**`adw_standalone`, one form** (ADD-A128, ledger queue #105). Every value the GNOME facts derive with it, the
roles `role.global.accent_standalone`, `role.global.status.<kind>.standalone` and `role.osd.negative`, `neutral` and
`positive`, and every value derived from them (a link colour, the focus ring's `alpha`, the visited link's `mix`, the
symbolic icons' palette), takes this one form, GTK's computed sRGB colour. After the value, GTK uses it three ways,
each a step of the drawing that no later CSS function reads: as it is, for the symbolic icons' colours and through
`gtk_widget_get_color` (`gtk@4.24.1 gtk/gtkcssstyle.c:886-895`, `gtk/gtkwidget.c:13458-13468`); clamped to `0..=1`
and rounded to 16 bits, for a label's link (`gtk/gtklabel.c:888-892`); and not at all for a label's or an entry's
text, a background, a border, an outline and a shadow, which are drawn from the OKLab coordinates the style keeps beside
it, and which the renderer converts to sRGB itself (`gtk/gtkrenderlayout.c:60`, `gtk/gtkrenderbackground.c:263`,
`gtk/gtkrenderborder.c:695-698`, `:761`, `gtk/gtkcssshadowvalue.c:608`, `gtk/gtkcsscolor.c:1214-1240`, `gdk/gdkcolorstate.c:359`), in single precision, the
cube as two products and the sRGB curve in single, mirrored for a negative channel (`gdk/gdkcolordefs.h:32-42`,
`:282-287`). That conversion is within 7.9·10⁻⁴ of this form on the 0–255 scale for the channels in gamut on spike
G's grid, and outside the gamut both agree to 2·10⁻⁴ once clamped (two emulations over the grid at alpha 1, the
stylesheet's origins being opaque; ledger queue #105); the renderer's 8-bit store
clamps and rounds each. No check compares a drawn colour finer than that: a vector row compares this form itself
(below), a published fact, at the quote check's precision, the preset's call of the same function, a read through `gtk_widget_get_color` this form,
and a capture rounds to 8 bits, by up to half a step, far above these differences (the link's 16-bit rounding is at most
2·10⁻³), while a render-node file (`.node`) a GNOME harness records holds an OKLab-drawn colour as its OKLab
coordinates, unrounded (`gsk/gskrendernodeparser.c:5445-5472`), which an analysis converts as this function does
before comparing. So the function has no second form: one per drawing path would split each role into two that differ, once
drawn, by less than a capture shows, which no connector's toolkit draws apart. Outside the gamut, where 16 of the
standalone colours libadwaita documents lie (the default blue's dark one has a blue channel of 1.218717, which
libadwaita notes is clipped before it is displayed, `doc/css-variables.md:89-92`, `:96-99`, the others marked at
`:140-438`), the value is clamped where it is drawn, as GTK clamps it (S2.1's hand-over): not by the function, which
would change an `alpha` or `mix` over an out-of-gamut colour (GTK's `color-mix()` and `alpha()` read the unclamped
channels, above), visibly on the focus ring, `alpha(role.global.accent_standalone, …)`, and by at most one step of 255
on the visited link's `mix`; nor at the end of resolution, which would clamp the focus ring's colour before its
alpha, where GTK's renderer premultiplies it first. **Its vectors** (`native-theme/tests/vectors/adw_standalone.tsv`):
route `observable_behaviour`, sources `gtk@4.24.1` and `libadwaita@1.10.0`, generation `adwaita`, generator
`tools/gnome-vectors` at those pins (their packages, S17), inputs `c:colour scheme:enum<Scheme>`, output
`result:colour`. The generator initialises libadwaita, forces each scheme through `AdwStyleManager`, names each input
colour with `@define-color`, written in CSS's `color()` notation in `srgb` from the row's exact singles, whose channels
GTK keeps unclamped and whose alpha it clamps to `0..=1` (`gtk/gtkcsscolorvalue.c:1701-1722`, `:1397-1426`; `rgb()`
clamps its channels, `:1389-1390`); the named origin keeps GTK on the path the roles' named origins take, where a
literal origin is computed when parsed and GTK clamps L to `0..=1` (`:1513-1535`, `:1946-1966`). It styles a widget's
colour as the stylesheet's relative colour of that origin with the stylesheet's own limit, `--standalone-color-oklab`,
and writes
`gtk_widget_get_color`'s four singles unrounded as `srgb(…)`. Its rows: spike G's grid (red, green and blue each
over 0, 51, 102, 153, 204 and 255, /255) at alpha 1 in both schemes, out-of-gamut results included; every
`AdwAccentColor` colour and the four status backgrounds of each scheme (`_colors.scss:11-22`, `:83-86`) at alpha 1,
0.75 and 0.5; inputs with a channel above 1 and below 0; inputs whose L lies within a single's step of 0.5 and of
0.85, and channels at the curve's thresholds, 0.04045 in and 0.0031308 out. The test `vectors_adw_standalone`
compares each output channel and the alpha unrounded on the 0–255 scale to 1e-3, as every generated table
(below); `check_function_vectors.py` checks the table's form and that its rows serve `adwaita` under both schemes, as
the facts call it with `scheme` and with `dark`. The route is the observed behaviour, not `compiled_source`: it runs
the stylesheet's whole path, the named origin, the limit and the storage included, on spike G's headless display,
where a harness calling GTK's internal conversion would skip that path; `tools/gnome-vectors` is rewritten to it. Spike G's table, `adw_rgba_to_standalone`'s through
its public API, clamps, and is not this function's table. The implementation follows the CSS Color 4 conversion
between sRGB and OKLab (W3C, followed directly, D10) and the stylesheet's limit as described here; GTK's constants
as singles, the precision of each step and its linear piece for negative channels, which are GTK's own and which the
1e-3 unrounded comparison needs reproduced, come from the clean room's description of this form (D10 a).

A function is added to this table only with the platform rule that needs it and its source (R5.4). How each KDE
function treats a translucent input (mixes, keeps or ignores alpha) is read from its source in the value phase and
recorded in its facts (R5.4). A platform
that computes a stored colour by composition (KDE's `overlayColors`) gets a function; composition drawn over what
lies beneath is a paint layer (R5.4, R6). Type checking: every operand and result is typed (*Typing*'s operand
types, above, `enum<E>`, shadow and paint among them); a name operand is checked against the enum or declared key
set the function's parameter names (`design: TrackingDesign`, `group: KdeGroup`, `role_kind: KdeRoleKind`, `kde_accent`'s `key: KdeSchemeKey`,
`kde_shade`'s `role: KdeShadeRole`, `uikit_prominence`'s `prominence: UiProminence`, `shadow_extent`'s `side: BoxSide`,
`kde_accent_wm`'s `key: KdeWmKey`;
`m3_role`'s `role` is a declared keyed colour role, `uifm_scaled`'s `text_role` a `TextRoles` slot or a declared text
style); in `add`, `sub`, `min`, `max` and each of `if_le`'s two pairs (`a` with `b`, `x` with `y`), and only there, a bare number takes the type of
the other operand (*Typing*; in `mul` and `div` a number operand stays a number, so `div(4px, 2)` is a length; ADD-A146); `mul(T, number)`, `div(T, number)`, `div(T, T)` (a number), `add(T, T)`, `sub(T, T)`, `min(T, T)`, `max(T, T)`, `floor(T)`, `ceil(T)` and `round(T)` give a `T`, `if_le(T, T, U, U)` a `U`, and `round_pt` takes and gives a font size;
where one operand of `add`, `sub`, `min` or `max`, or of either of `if_le`'s pairs, is a font size and the other a length, the length is taken as px
and the result is a font size (S2.2's operand types, as M1a task 2 implemented it, ADD-A121): in `if_le` the result of `(x, y)`, its `(a, b)` giving no result, so that there the rule says only how the two are compared (ADD-A147);
a mismatch is an error when the layer is added (S12). A function that reads inputs or reader values itself
(`kde_accent` reads `input.accent`, `input.kde_scheme.<set>.<key>`, `.<set>.inactive.<key>`, `.<set>.background_normal`,
`.window.<key>`, `.window.background_normal`, `.view.background_normal`, `.groups`, `.inactive_groups` and
`.unset_keys`, `token.kde.tint_factor` and `titlebar_is_accent_colored`, every one stated, S4.8, S9.1, and holds
KColorScheme's two `Header` default backgrounds as cited constants (`kcolorscheme.cpp:200-203`; its other ten `Header`
defaults equal `input.kde_scheme.window.<key>` wherever `Window`'s key is unset); which roles depend on the accent is
S9.1's list; `kde_accent_wm` reads `input.accent`,
`input.kde_scheme.wm.<key>`, `input.kde_scheme.window.background_normal`, `.groups` and `.unset_keys` (a file with no
`[Colors:Window]` group leaves `Window`'s background unset without naming it in `unset_keys`) and the same two tokens;
the clean-room description `briefs/kde-accent-descriptions.md`, §5, §10; ADD-A142; `uifm_scaled` the reader's content-size
category, S8, S9.4; `round_pt` `token.text.font_dpi` and the reader's `font_dpi`, S9.4) lists them, and the checks treat them as its operands. A font size reaches a function in logical
pixels, converted and scaled (S9.4), except in an expression stated on a `Font.size` (a part's `text.font.size`, a
text style token's), where every font-size operand (another style's or slot's `font.size`, `widget.<part>.font_size`)
is converted and not yet scaled, and the result is scaled once (S9.4); a `FontSize` widget value, not text-scaled
(S1), reads its font-size operands converted only. `floor`, `ceil` and `round` take a font size so, in px, and `if_le` compares one so (ADD-A147); `round_pt` rounds it in points (the table above; ADD-A131).

**Totality** (the query cannot fail, R2.8): `alpha` clamps the resulting alpha to `0..=1`, as CSS Color 5's relative
colours do (a factor above one is valid: libadwaita multiplies a shade's alpha by more, GN-1.210); `with_alpha` clamps `a` to `0..=1`, as
`QColor::setAlphaF` and CSS do; `mix` clamps its
fraction to `0..=1`; `pick` floors the index and takes its Euclidean remainder by the number of its colours, at least
one (S12); every count operand of zero is one (`name_index`, `kqc_series_color`); a length or duration that comes out
negative where the field cannot be negative is zero; a computed `Material.saturation`, `MotionTokens.speed_factor` or
spring `time_scale` below zero is zero; a number that becomes an integer (a `Value<u16>` weight, a `Value<u32>`
count) is floored and clamped to the integer type's range, a negative one to zero; a loop whose period evaluates to
zero does not run (the part shows its style without the loop's keyframes: R9's animations off sets the speed factor,
and so a scaled period, to zero); `if_le` compares two finite values, every operand being finite (a non-finite
result, or non-finite element data, is zero, below), so it always selects (ADD-A147); a non-finite result, or
non-finite element data, is zero. A platform function
follows its source's own clamping first. No function clamps a colour's channels unless its source does, `Color`
holding them outside `0..=1` (S2.1): `alpha` and `mix` keep them, as GTK's `alpha()` and `color-mix()` do
(`gtk@4.24.1 gtk/gtkcsscolorvalue.c:556-564`, `gtk/gtkcsscolor.c:919-970`). An expression naming `element.<data>` is re-evaluated by each
query, so a connector queries again when the data changes, as for a state (R25.3).

**Checked against their references** (ADD-A113). Each platform function has a vector table under
`native-theme/tests/vectors/`, built from its reference at the pinned release (S17's `sources.toml`), each reference by one of three routes, recorded with the table: the reference's public API; its observable behaviour through public API; or the
pinned upstream source compiled unchanged in a CI tool that calls the internal function (never part of the crate).
Where the reference is closed, measured inputs and outputs, each with its evidence (S17), are the table; where a
platform publishes a table (Apple's tracking), that table is the vector table, its rows carrying S17's citations.
S9.4's scaling curves (`AndroidNonLinear`, `DynamicType`, `WinUi`) are checked the same way. The model's own arithmetic
(`alpha`, `with_alpha`, `mix`, `mul`, `div`, `add`, `sub`, `min`, `max`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `round_pt`, `if_le`, `pick`; ADD-A147) is not a platform function: its unit tests
follow this section's definitions; every other function of the table above is one. A vector table, under `native-theme/tests/vectors/`,
holds rows of inputs and outputs. Each row is traceable to the reference as a fact is (S17): generated by it (the
generator a CI tool at a pinned source), published by it (citations whose quotes hold the row's literals), or
measured on it (evidence as S17's, holding the inputs the harness set or read and the outputs it measured). A
function row's citations, evidence or generator's pin together serve each generation whose presets use the function
with that row's enum operands; a row for an enum operand no preset uses is checked over all its citations, evidence and
generator's pin. The quote check runs
per generation. Generated outputs compare unrounded, colours on the 0–255 scale to 1e-3 (but S2.5's
`kirigami_shadow_alpha`, a GPU shader on a pinned renderer, within its header's tolerance; ADD-A135), so an implementation
reproduces the reference's intermediate storage (QColor's 16-bit channels and integer HSV). A function whose
reference differs by generation or platform selects it by an enum operand, as `name_index`'s `method` does (a class 2
change where a lane finds such a difference), so one implementation answers every row; every preset whose facts or
preset files call the function is served by its rows.

A placement strategy's row names its preset and the value it places (the field path, with its rule's selector as
S11's `when`: `combo_box.values.popup_placement` with `{ variants = ["@pull_down"] }`), serves that preset's
generation only, and takes its `PlacementParams` from that preset resolved under that `when` (its conditions and
flavour in force, the gate's default stand-in otherwise, S17), not from columns. Every value of
every preset that names the strategy has rows; a strategy no preset names (one an application's layer may choose,
such as `material-3`'s `KeyboardAvoid` strategies by `softInputMode`) has rows for a preset of its platform, which
the row names as above.

A test evaluates each function and strategy over its table. `scripts/check_function_vectors.py` holds, documents and
self-tests the table's file format (header lines naming the routes, the sources and generations, the columns and
their types, the tolerances), and checks that every platform function of the table above, every function
implementing S9.4's curves and every `pub` or `pub(crate)` function of the `platform` module has a table and a test,
and that every platform function a fact or a preset names is one of them; `check_fact_citations.py` checks the rows'
citations and counts their evidence as cited.

**The readers' helpers** (ADD-A135; ledger queue #172). A reader's parser or classifier ported from an LGPL source
through the clean room (the 0.8.0 plan's D10) is no platform function, as no fact or preset calls it, and is checked as
one is: a vector table `native-theme/tests/vectors/reader.<helper>.tsv`, by one of the routes above, its
`generations` the reader's own preset, and a test `vectors_reader_<helper>`, a unit test in the helper's own module
reading that table (the helper is `pub(crate)`, which `native-theme/tests/platform_vectors.rs` cannot call).
The helpers are exactly these, each a `pub(crate)` function of the reader module that uses it: `pango_font_description`
(the GNOME reader's, Pango's `pango_font_description_from_string`, `pango@1.58.2 pango/fonts.c:1613-1729`, read for
the gsettings font strings), `qfont_from_string` (the KDE reader's, Qt's `QFont::fromString`, `qtbase@6.12.0
src/gui/text/qfont.cpp:2246-2320`, for kdeglobals' font entries), `adw_accent_nearest` (the GNOME reader's,
libadwaita's `adw_accent_color_nearest_from_rgba`, `libadwaita@1.10.0 src/adw-accent-color.c:159-199`, S9.3),
`kde_color_scheme` (the KDE reader's, Plasma's dark-or-light test of the palette's window colour, plasma-integration's
`KHintsSettings::determineColorScheme` and xdg-desktop-portal-kde's `readFdoColorScheme` over Qt's `qGray`,
`plasma-integration@6.8.2 qt6/src/platformtheme/khintssettings.cpp:469-485`, `xdg-desktop-portal-kde@6.8.2
src/settings.cpp:259-273`, `qtbase@6.12.0 src/gui/painting/qrgb.h:37-38`, `:40-41`, S9.3; ADD-A140, its lines
corrected by ADD-A141) and `qxcb_xft_dpi` (the
KDE reader's, Qt's xcb plugin reading `Xft.dpi` from the X resources, `qtbase@6.12.0
src/plugins/platforms/xcb/qxcbscreen.cpp:298-314`, `:366-373`, `:856-876`, S9.3; ADD-A140; withdrawn by ADD-A146,
the KDE reader reporting no font DPI, S9.4's *What the toolkit's scale carries*: listed until its implementation and
its table are removed, a code follow-up).
`check_function_vectors.py` reads this list as it reads S2.2's functions: a listed helper with a table and no
implementation is reported as waiting (its implementer receives the table first, D10); an implemented one without
its table or test is a finding, and so is a `reader.` table of a name not listed. A table's columns may take the type
`string`, a JSON string literal (RFC 8259), which, unlike `text`, holds the empty string, surrounding whitespace, tabs
and newlines, the inputs these parsers meet (`""`, `"\tSans\t11"`). Rejected: the helpers in S2.2's table of
functions (each would become an expression function a fact or preset could call, while it parses or classifies
what a reader reads and derives no value); no table (D10 makes the table the implementer's only reference); `text` cells with escapes (a second
escaping scheme beside JSON's, which the generators already write).

### S2.3 Paint (R6)

```rust
pub struct Paint { pub layers: Vec<PaintLayer> }             // bottom first; at least one layer (S12);
                                                             // "paints nothing" is `Value::Absent`
pub struct PaintLayer { pub kind: PaintKind, pub blend: BlendMode }
pub enum PaintKind {
    Color(Value<Color>),
    Linear { angle: Deg, stops: Vec<Stop>, repeat: bool,
             extent: Option<Value<Px>>,       // stops over this many px from the start edge (ADD-A31); None: the box
             offset: Option<Value<Px>> },     // the stops shifted along the axis by this many px (K1.110); None:
                                              // not shifted
    Radial { center: (f32, f32), radius: Value<Px>, stops: Vec<Stop>, repeat: bool },  // center: fractions of
                                                                                        // the box; radius in px
    Conic { center: (f32, f32), start_angle: Deg, stops: Vec<Stop> },          // R25.4
    Pattern { pattern: Pattern, foreground: Value<Color>, background: Value<Color>,  // R25.4; the grid's lines
              cell: Value<Px> },                                                  // are its foreground
    Material(Material),
}
pub enum Pattern { Checkerboard, Grid, QtBrush(QtBrushStyle) }   // each to its platform's source (R25.4)
pub enum QtBrushStyle { Dense1, Dense2, Dense3, Dense4, Dense5, Dense6, Dense7, Hor, Ver, Cross, BDiag, FDiag,
                        DiagCross }                               // Qt's `Qt::BrushStyle` patterns
pub struct Stop { pub position: f32, pub color: Value<Color> }
pub enum BlendMode { Normal, Mask,           // Mask: the layer's alpha masks the layers beneath it (below)
                     Difference,             // CSS's `difference` against what lies beneath (below; ADD-A134)
                     Keyed(Key) }            // platform blending modes as the facts name them (macOS vibrancy)
pub struct Material {
    pub identity: Key,                        // the platform's material (S10 declares the set)
    pub blur_radius: Value<Px>,
    pub tint: Value<Color>,
    pub saturation: Value<f32>,               // a multiplier, at least zero (CSS `saturate()`, K3.11)
    pub luminosity: Value<Fraction>,
    pub noise_opacity: Value<Fraction>,
    pub fallback: Value<Color>,               // what a toolkit that cannot draw it draws (R6)
    pub params: Vec<(Key, Value<Scalar>)>,    // what a platform's material states beyond these (ADD-A47)
}
```

A rule's patch either sets a paint (`fill = …`) or appends layers over `base` (`fill.append = [ … ]`) (R6). Angles
follow CSS: `Linear.angle` is `linear-gradient()`'s angle, `0deg` pointing toward the top of the box and angles
increasing clockwise; `Conic.start_angle` is `conic-gradient()`'s `from` angle on the same convention, its stops
running clockwise from it. A gradient has at least two stops (S12): one colour is a `Color` layer, the one route. A
repeating gradient repeats its stops beyond the last (stripes, K1.110). A linear gradient's `offset` moves its stops
along its axis, toward the axis's end for a positive offset (a repeating one wraps; a non-repeating one extends its
end colours, as without an offset), so a loop's keyframes, or a transition, that change it move the pattern: Breeze's
busy stripes, offset by one pattern period over the loop (K1.110). It interpolates as a length. A paint is drawn in
the box's own coordinates and is not mirrored in right-to-left, as a CSS gradient is not; a platform that reverses
one there (Breeze's stripes run the other way, `breezehelper.cpp:1245-1247`) states it by a rule under the direction
(S7, R16). Corners, stroke edges and shadow offsets are physical likewise (S2.4, S2.5).

A layer with `BlendMode::Mask` is not drawn: its alpha, at each point, multiplies the alpha of the layers beneath it
in the same paint (Porter-Duff destination-in, CSS's `mask` with an alpha mask), so a gradient from opaque to
transparent stated over a `Material` layer fades the material out (Apple 26's soft scroll edge, MAC-X05, C-18;
`scroll_view.edge_effect`); the layers above it are drawn normally. A paint whose bottom
layer is a `Mask` masks nothing and is refused (S12).

A layer with `BlendMode::Difference` (ADD-A134) is drawn with CSS Compositing's `difference` blend (W3C Compositing
and Blending Level 1, followed directly) against its backdrop, everything drawn beneath it at that point: the
paint's layers below it and, beneath the part, what the part's ancestors, the parts beneath it and the text it
covers have drawn. Each channel is `|backdrop − layer|` on straight sRGB values, composited by the layer's alpha
as CSS composites a blended source. An opaque white layer so draws the inverse of what lies beneath, which is
WinUI's caret: a white rectangle (`DefaultCaretColor`) composited with `ElementCompositeMode::DestInvert`, the
composition mode under which "the visual content's colors are inverted" (`microsoft-ui-xaml@2.5.1
src/dxaml/xcp/core/native/text/Controls/TextBoxView.cpp:2771-2800`, `src/dxaml/xcp/components/comptree/HWCompNodeWinRT.cpp:2706-2707`;
`winapps-winrt-api@554b7e3a microsoft.ui.composition/compositioncompositemode.md:22-23`), so `windows-11`'s
`token.caret.color` is that white and each caret part's `fill` is one layer of it under `Difference` (S4.2). Qt's
widget caret, where its paint engine has raster operations and its target no alpha channel, is drawn with
`QPainter::RasterOp_NotDestination`, which inverts what lies beneath whatever the pen's colour, as a white
`Difference` layer does; on a target with an alpha channel it draws the pen's colour (`qtbase@6.12.0
src/gui/text/qtextlayout.cpp:1362-1375`): which path a Breeze window takes is the KDE lane's to settle (ADD-A134's
follow-ups). A toolkit that cannot blend a layer records it as its limit (R23). Rejected: a `Caret.color` form
`Inverse` (a colour type with a member that is no colour, which the caret parts' `= token.caret.color` and every
expression over the caret's colour could not take, and a second home for blending, which is the paint layer's);
a keyed blend `@dest_invert` (the existing route, but the operation is defined and two platforms draw it, so a
connector would map one key per platform for one operation and the gate could not compose it); a new block, a part's
composite mode as WinUI's `UIElement.CompositeMode` sets it (a field on every part for what one layer of the caret's
own fill states); the caret stated inexactly, white or the text's colour (white vanishes over a light field, the
text's colour differs over a selection or a dark background).

**A layer over the border** (ADD-A134). A part's `fill` is drawn beneath its stroke (S2.11's *Drawing order*), so a layer the platform draws
over the whole box, its border included, is appended to the `fill` and to the paint of each drawn edge alike: both
are drawn in the box's coordinates (above), so a gradient so appended has the same colour at a border pixel in
either, and the border shows it over its own colour as the platform draws it. qqc2-desktop-style's `RoundButton`
draws its gloss, a vertical gradient, as a child rectangle filling its background, so over its border
(`qqc2-desktop-style@6.31.0 org.kde.desktop/RoundButton.qml:94-106`; Q2.6): `kde-breeze` appends the gloss to
`button.body.fill` and to each edge's `paint` under the same rule. The result is exact at every fully covered border pixel while the border is opaque
(the border's colour is `kirigami_lerp` of the button set's background and foreground); a translucent border would
show the fill's gloss through it once more. Rejected:
the border left unglossed as a recorded inexactness (up to the gloss's alpha on every border pixel, visible); a
paint layer drawn over the stroke, a new field or layer order (for what the edges' own paints already state).

### S2.4 Corners, stroke (R7)

```rust
pub struct Corners { pub top_left: Radius, pub top_right: Radius, pub bottom_right: Radius,
                     pub bottom_left: Radius, pub curve: CornerCurve }
pub enum Radius {
    Px(Value<Px>),
    Full { maximum: Value<Px> },          // a capsule: half the smaller side of the part's box (a ring's: its
                                          // inner box, S2.10), at most `maximum`
                                          // (UIKit's `capsule(maximumRadius:)`, X-CR-2); `maximum` may be absent
    Ellipse,                              // a quarter of the ellipse inscribed in the part's box: half its
                                          // width across, half its height down (below; ADD-A124)
    Concentric { minimum: Value<Px> },    // the container's radius less the inset, at least `minimum` (R7);
                                          // `minimum` may be absent
    FollowPart,                           // a focus indicator's: the part's radius plus the offset, concentric
}                                         // (R12); only in `FocusIndicator.corners`, and refused where the
                                          // corner's two sides' offsets differ (S12)
pub enum CornerCurve { Circular, Continuous }
pub struct Stroke { pub top: Edge, pub right: Edge, pub bottom: Edge, pub left: Edge,
                    pub position: StrokePosition,
                    pub outset: Value<Px>,       // the gap between the box and an `Outside` stroke (iOS's
                                                 // `strokeOutset`, CD-1); absent on an `Inside` or `Center`
                                                 // stroke only, where it has no meaning (below; ADD-A146)
                    pub fill_clip: FillClip }    // how far the part's fill reaches under the stroke (ADD-A121)
pub struct Edge { pub width: Value<Px>, pub paint: Value<Paint>, pub dash: Value<DashPattern>,   // ADD-A32
                  pub snap: PixelSnap }                                                    // ADD-A33
pub enum DashPattern { Solid, Dotted, Dashed { on: Px, off: Px } }   // a drawn edge states its pattern, `solid`
                                                                    // included: the one route for a solid line;
                                                                    // `dash` is absent only on an edge not drawn
                                                                    // (S6.3)
pub enum PixelSnap { None, ToDevicePixel, AtLeastOneDevicePixel }   // the width stays logical
pub enum LineCap { Butt, Round, Square }
pub enum LineJoin { Miter, Round, Bevel }
pub enum StrokePosition { Inside, Center, Outside }
pub enum FillClip { Box, InnerEdge, Center }   // Center: to the stroke's centre line (below; ADD-A135)
```

A part's outline is its `corners`, unless `PartStyle.shape` names a shape: `ShapeKind { Material(MaterialShape) }`, a
closed set implemented once in native-theme to `androidx.graphics.shapes` and `MaterialShapes.kt` at a pinned commit
(R25.5). `MaterialShape`'s variants are exactly the shapes `MaterialShapes.kt` defines at that commit, in that file's
order, each named as the file names it, in `UpperCamelCase` (TOML: snake_case, S11); the value phase writes the list
from the file when it pins the commit (it is not stated here, as no source for it was read). The shapes are code, as
placement strategies are (R16), in `native_theme::shapes`:

```rust
pub struct Path { pub commands: Vec<PathCommand> }   // in `Px`, in the coordinates of the `rect` it was made for;
                                                     // each `MoveTo` starts a closed outline; filled by the
                                                     // non-zero rule
pub enum PathCommand { MoveTo(Point), LineTo(Point), QuadTo(Point, Point), CubicTo(Point, Point, Point), Close }
                                                     // QuadTo: control, end; CubicTo: two controls, end
pub enum Outline { Corners(OutlineCorners), Shape(ShapeKind) }
pub struct OutlineCorners { pub radii: [Px; 4],          // every radius as the connector computed it at layout (a
                            pub curve: CornerCurve }     // stated `Radius::Px`, or S2.4's functions), in the order
                                                         // top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left
pub fn outline(shape: &ShapeKind, rect: Rect) -> Path;
pub fn morph(a: &Outline, b: &Outline, t: Fraction, rect: Rect) -> Option<Path>;   // t = 0: `a`, t = 1: `b`;
                                                     // None where either is `Corners` with a `Continuous` curve
```

As an `Outline`, a part is `Shape` where its `shape` is stated, else `Corners`, whose path is the rounded
rectangle `androidx.graphics.shapes` builds from the four radii (`RoundedPolygon.rectangle`), which draws circular
corners only. So a `Corners` outline is defined for `CornerCurve::Circular`: a part whose `shape` can be stated is
refused where its corners' curve can be `Continuous` (S12; only `material-3` states shapes, and its corners are
circular), so the model never asks `morph` for a continuous outline, and a direct call with one gets `None`. An `Interpolate`
transition of the `Shape` group (R25.5's transition of kind morph) morphs from the old outline to the new, so a
change between plain corners and a shape morphs too; a change of corners alone, with no shape on either side, is
the `Corners` group's.

`Full`, `Ellipse`, `Concentric` and `FollowPart` resolve as they are; the connector computes each such corner at
layout, from its own layout's numbers, with the pure functions of `native_theme::corners`:

```rust
pub fn full(width: Px, height: Px, maximum: Option<Px>) -> Px;                  // half the smaller side, at most
                                                                                // `maximum`
pub fn ellipse(width: Px, height: Px) -> Axes<Px>;                              // half the width across, half the
                                                                                // height down
pub fn concentric(container_radius: Px, inset: Axes<Px>, minimum: Option<Px>) -> Option<Px>;   // None: unequal
                                                                                // insets (below)
pub fn follow_part(part_radius: Px, offset: Px) -> Px;                          // part_radius + offset, at least 0
```

A `Concentric` corner's container is the nearest enclosing part or element whose catalogue entry lists `corners`,
decided by the catalogue, not by resolved values (a root that lists no corners, one that draws nothing, is skipped;
a full-screen part's container is the display, S4.6). The container's own corners may be `Full` or
`Concentric`, numbers only after layout (iOS 26 nests concentric containers): the `Scope` identifies
the container and holds its stated corners (S8), and the connector passes as `container_radius` the radius it
computed for the container's matching corner, which it has, as it lays out and queries top-down. A square container,
or the display with no radius (S4.6), passes 0, so the corner is its minimum, or square without one. `inset` is, per
axis, the part's stated distance from the container's edge on that corner's side: the container's `padding` on that
side, the `margin` and `padding` on that side of every part between them, and the part's own `margin` there, resolved (so mirrored as `Sides`
are, S2.4), not the part's laid-out position: a floating part's distance from the window is its `margin` (the
catalogue's floating sidebar pane, toolbar and tab bar, SD-6, MAC-SB06, MAT-N25, T-9). The connector sums it from the resolved styles it
queried on its way down, the `Scope` naming the container (S8). So every part held in the container's padding follows its corner
(libadwaita draws each toggle of a toggle group, the middle ones included, at the group's radius less the group's
padding, `libadwaita@1.10.0 src/stylesheet/widgets/_toggle-group.scss:10-14`, `:29`, GN-1.239). `concentric` returns the
larger of `container_radius` less the inset and `minimum` (0 when absent) where the two insets are equal. Concentric
corners are Apple's (iOS 26, macOS 26), so where the insets differ `concentric` will follow UIKit's rule, stated as
UIKit's: read in the value phase from `UICornerConfiguration` and `UIView.effectiveRadius(corner:)` (X-CR-2) and cited
in the function's doc comment, which also settles whether UIKit measures the laid-out position instead (a class 2
change if it does). Until then `concentric` returns `None` for unequal insets (ADD-A122) rather than inventing a rule,
and S12 refuses a layer whose `Concentric` corner can have unequal insets, the paddings and margins on its two sides
followed through references and rules conservatively, as a `FollowPart` corner's offsets are, so a connector never
meets that `None`; the value phase's rule replaces both (another platform's concentric corners, a full-screen window
following the display, MAT-W5†, sit at no inset).

**The elliptical corner** (`Radius::Ellipse`, R7, ADD-A124). Each corner is a quarter of the ellipse inscribed in the
part's box, its radii half the box's width across and half its height down, so a square box is a circle, as `Full`
draws it. It is Breeze's QWidget round button: Breeze gives `drawRoundedRect` a radius of half the larger side of
the button's rect (`breeze@6.8.2 kstyle/breezehelper.cpp:727`, `:738-739`), which Qt clamps per axis to half each side
of the frame rect it draws (`QPainter::drawRoundedRect` hands it to the paint engine, `qtbase@6.12.0
src/gui/painting/qpainter.cpp:4015-4018`, which clamps it, `qpaintengineex.cpp:745-746`; the path fallback likewise,
`qpainterpath.cpp:3457-3470`), the inscribed ellipse
whenever that rect is not square. An `Ellipse` part states it on all four corners with a `Circular` curve (S12 refuses
a mix and `Continuous`), as Breeze, its one source, draws it: the four corners of one ellipse, circular where the box
is square. Wherever the model takes a corner's radii less an inset (a stroke's inner edge, the fill under `InnerEdge`,
an inset shadow's box), it takes the horizontal radius less the inset on the corner's vertical side and the vertical
radius less the inset on its horizontal side, each at least 0, as CSS reduces an elliptical corner, so equal insets
give the ellipse inscribed in the inset box; where the model grows the box (an `Outside` stroke's or a `Center`
stroke's outer edge, an outset), it adds each axis's outset to that axis's radius likewise (*Growing an outline*,
below). A `Corners` transition into or out of `Ellipse` interpolates each
corner's horizontal and vertical radii, a circular corner's two being equal, as CSS interpolates `border-radius`. An
`Ellipse` part has no `Outline`, whose `OutlineCorners` hold one radius per corner: a part whose `shape` can be stated
is refused where its corners can be `Ellipse` (S12), as where they can be `Continuous`.

**Growing an outline** (ADD-A136; ledger queue #174 (1), #175). Wherever the model grows a part's outline by a
distance (an `Outside` stroke's outer edge by its `outset` and width, a `Center` stroke's by half its width, an outer
shadow layer's shape by a positive `spread` and an inset layer's inner shape by a negative one, S2.5), each corner
radius above zero grows by that distance, an `Ellipse` corner's radius on each axis by the distance on that axis's
side, and a zero radius stays zero, a square corner square; a radius above zero but below the distance grows by the
whole of it too. Where it shrinks the outline, each radius is less the distance, at least 0 (above). It is the outline's
outer offset with its arcs concentric and its square corners kept square (a mitred join), as GTK grows a rounded
rectangle for an outline or a shadow (`gtk@4.24.1 gtk/gtkcssboxesimplprivate.h:495-504`; a border it shrinks inward
from the border box): a radius changed only where it is above zero
(`gtk@4.24.1 gsk/gskroundedrect.c:217-236`; the GPU renderer's `rounded_rect_shrink` by the radius's sign,
`gsk/gpu/shaders/roundedrect.glsl:92-101`; the shadows, `gsk/gskoutsetshadownode.c:117`,
`gsk/gskinsetshadownode.c:92`, `gsk/gpu/shaders/gskgpuboxshadow.glsl:37-51`). A focus ring's corners keep S2.10's own
rule (`follow_part` grows a square corner, as CSS's outline does), as they are stated there. Rejected: the distance
added to every radius, a square corner included (a rounded corner GTK does not draw there); CSS
Backgrounds 3's spread factor, the distance times `1 + (r − 1)³` for a radius below it, `r` the radius over the
distance (*Shadow shape*), which a browser's box shadow applies: `material-3`'s elevations are material-web's CSS
box shadows (`material-web@2.5.0 elevation/internal/_elevation.scss:107-112`, ambient spreads 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 px at
levels 1 to 5, `docs/facts/material/tokens.toml:1381-1521`), but the one `material-3` part that takes a shadow, the
button's body, never has a radius above zero and below its spread: its levels reach level4 (4 px, a hovered `@fab`
or `@extended_fab`), and its corners are at least `token.params.shape.small`, 8 px, or a capsule, half the smaller
side of a box at least 28 px wide and 32 px high (`docs/facts/material/button.toml`), so CSS's factor, 1 for a radius
at or above the spread, changes nothing there, and GTK's rule holds for every bundled preset (`adwaita`'s growing
layers GTK draws; `kde-breeze`'s spreads are negative, `windows-11`'s one inset layer shrinks its hole); a preset part
meeting the case adds the factor then (a class 2 change); a field choosing the rule per layer (a member no preset
uses).

**The fill under the stroke** (`Stroke.fill_clip`, ADD-A121). With `Box` the part's fill covers its whole box (the
outline), beneath the part of the stroke that lies inside the box (an `Inside` stroke, the inner half of a `Center`
one): CSS's default `background-clip: border-box`, WinUI's `BackgroundSizing="OuterBorderEdge"`
(`microsoft-ui-xaml@2.5.1 src/controls/dev/CommonStyles/Button_themeresources.xaml:238`, `AccentButtonStyle`), a Qt
painter's brush under a pen drawn on the box's own outline (a `Center` stroke). With `InnerEdge` the fill stops at the stroke's inner edge, inset
on each edge by the part of that edge's width that lies inside the box (all of it for `Inside`, half for `Center`,
none for `Outside`), its corners the outline's radii less that inset, at least 0, as CSS's padding-box corners are:
CSS's `background-clip: padding-box`, WinUI's `InnerBorderEdge` (`Button_themeresources.xaml:156`, the default
button; `ToggleButton_themeresources.xaml:182`, with `OuterBorderEdge` while checked but not disabled, `:6`,
`:255-256`, its `CheckedDisabled` state setting none, `:292-304`; AppBarToggleButton's in all four checked states,
`AppBarToggleButton_themeresources.xaml:343`, `:354`, `:367`, `:380`; ADD-A122). With `Center` (ADD-A135; ledger
queue #165) the fill stops at the stroke's centre line where that line lies inside the box: inset on each edge by
half that edge's width for an `Inside` stroke, by none for a `Center` one (as `Box`) or an `Outside` one (the fill
never leaves the box), its corners the outline's radii less that inset, at least 0, as for `InnerEdge`. It is a Qt
painter's brush under a pen on a rectangle inset by half the pen's width, Breeze's button frame: the brush and the
pen on one painter, one rounded rectangle, the box inset by half the pen width, its radius the frame radius less half
the pen width, so the pen lies inside the box and the fill reaches its centre line (`breeze@6.8.2
kstyle/breezehelper.cpp:670-671`, `:736-739`, `:1747-1757`; `breezehelper.h:345-348`; U680). Rejected: Breeze's stroke
stated `Center` with `Box` (it would move the pen's outer half outside the box); `Box` or `InnerEdge` as a known
inexactness (the difference shows under a see-through pen, Breeze's flat button fading its hover pen,
`breezehelper.cpp:714-725`); a fill inset of its own length (a field for one platform's half width). The
difference shows where the stroke is translucent (WinUI's elevation strokes, W1-018). A stroke `Absent` has no
`fill_clip`: the fill covers the box. A change of it is a change of a value with no interpolation (an enum; S2.7's
*A value with no interpolation*): at once where no transition times the `Stroke` group, else as its run leaves its
delay.

**The outset** (`Stroke.outset`; ADD-A146). On an `Outside` stroke it is a length, `0px` where the stroke lies at
the box's edge, a platform with no such property stating that zero by omission, cited as an absence (S17), never
`Absent`: an `Outside` stroke with no gap is one look and has one spelling, as a text with no added spacing has
(S6.3). On an `Inside` or `Center` stroke, which no gap moves, the field has no meaning and is `Absent`, its one
spelling there (S12 refuses an outset `Absent` where the stroke's `position` is `Outside` and stated where it is
not).

TOML shorthands: `corners_px = <n>` sets the four corners to the plain radius `Radius::Px` (no other variant has a
shorthand: a capsule states each corner, `top_left = { full = { maximum_px = … } }`, S11); the curve beside it is
`corners.curve`, the one second key S12 accepts for that field. The `stroke` table's shorthand keys `width_px`,
`paint`, `dash` and `snap` each set that field on all four edges; the table's other keys are `position`,
`outset_px`, `fill_clip` and the edges' own tables (`top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left`). A table is written either with dotted keys
(`stroke.width_px = <n>`, `stroke.paint = "…"`, `stroke.dash = "solid"`, `stroke.snap = "to_device_pixel"`,
`stroke.position = "inside"`, `stroke.outset_px = "absent"`, `stroke.fill_clip = "box"`) or as one inline table holding
every key it states (`stroke = { width_px = <n>, paint = "…", dash = "solid", snap = "to_device_pixel", position = "inside",
outset_px = "absent", fill_clip = "box" }`), never both, as TOML cannot extend an inline table. An edge's table states no field a shorthand key sets (a
duplicate key, S12): an edge that differs is stated with all four edges' tables and no shorthand.

Where two drawn edges meet, the corner square (or, under rounded corners, the corner's arc) is painted once, never
by both edges, so a translucent stroke's corner is no darker than its sides: where the two edges' paints and widths
are equal it is that edge's; where they differ it is divided between them along the line from the outer corner to
the inner one, as CSS divides a border's corner between two border colours, each half painted by its own edge (and
dashed by its own pattern).

**Right-to-left.** A `Corners`' corners (`top_left` …) and a `Stroke`'s edges (`top` … `left`) are physical: they
are not mirrored under right-to-left, as CSS's physical `border-*-radius` and `border-*` properties are not, and
neither is a shadow's `x` offset (S2.5). A platform that mirrors one of them (a segmented control's first segment
rounding its start corners in either direction, a sidebar pane's stroke on its content side) states it by a rule
under the direction (`dir rtl`, S7). What mirrors with the layout is the layout's own geometry, `Sides` (S1),
every value naming a horizontal end of the layout by `Start`, `End`, `Leading` or `Trailing` (*Who mirrors*, below:
`Alignment` and the catalogue's other enums; placement, S13: `PlacementSide`, `PlacementAlign`, and its `Sides`; a
presentation's start or end edge, `EdgeSide`), and of a part's drawing only a
translation (a transform's `translate_x`, a presentation's `Translate.dx`), for S2.6's reason: it is a displacement
in the mirrored layout, while a corner, an edge, a transform's origin or a light source belongs to the drawing.

**Who mirrors: the query.** Values are stated for a left-to-right layout; the query returns them physical, already
mirrored for the element's direction (its own, else its scope's, S8): for `rtl` it swaps `left` and `right` in
`Sides`, negates `translate_x` and `Translate.dx`, and swaps `Start` with `End` and `Leading` with `Trailing`
wherever a part style, a widget value or a token it returns for the element holds a variant so named, of the
core's `EdgeSide`, `PlacementSide` and `PlacementAlign` and of every enum the catalogue declares (its shared value
types, `Alignment` and `Side` among them, and each entry's own). The test is the variant's name (ADD-A146): the
word alone or one of the words of an `UpperCamelCase` name is swapped for its counterpart (`Start` and `End`,
`Leading` and `Trailing`, `TopEnd` and `TopStart`, `EndColumn` and `StartColumn`, `TrailingInline` and
`LeadingInline`; `BothEnds` holds none of the four). So in those enums the four words name a horizontal end of the
layout and nothing else, and every variant holding one has its counterpart in the same enum, which
`scripts/generate_widgets.py --check` refuses a catalogue enum without; a counterpart no preset states for the
left-to-right layout is there as the query's right-to-left result. The `vertical` member of an `Axes` is not
swapped, a vertical alignment's `Start` being the top in either direction, and neither is a text's `Elision`
(S2.8), whose `Start` and `End` are the text's own ends and follow the text's direction, not the layout's (as
Pango's ellipsize modes name them, `pango@1.58.2 pango/pango-layout.h:100-102`). So in a resolved value `left`,
`Start` and `Leading` are the physical left. Rejected: the swap only in an enum holding both words whole (the
generator's first test: it left `TopEnd` and `EndColumn` logical beside a physical `Side::End`, two meanings of one word
in resolved values, with no list telling a connector which enums it must mirror itself); every start and end value
returned logical, numbers alone mirrored (it reopens ADD-A112, and each connector then mirrors what its toolkit
does not). A
rule under `dir rtl` states these values the same way, for the left-to-right layout, and the query mirrors them with
the rest, so a platform that keeps one unmirrored states its mirror image there (a translation kept: the rule's
`translate_x` negated); the physical values (corners, stroke edges, shadow offsets, paints, the origin) a rule under
the direction states as drawn. A connector draws what it receives and never mirrors these again: where its toolkit mirrors start and end values itself
(Qt's and GTK's layouts), it passes them in the toolkit's physical form (Qt's `AlignAbsolute`) or turns that
mirroring off, and its contract records which (S21.3). `place()` takes the parameters so resolved and does not mirror
them again (S13). A corner that reads a `Sides` value (a `FollowPart` corner's offsets, S2.10) reads the resolved,
physical members on its own edges.

### S2.5 Shadow (R8)

```rust
pub enum Shadow { Layers(Vec<ShadowLayer>), Elevation(Key) }   // Key: an entry of the elevation ramp (S4), which
                                                                 // may be empty (Material's level 0: no shadow);
                                                                 // `Layers` has at least one; no shadow is `Absent`
pub struct ShadowLayer { pub x: Value<Px>, pub y: Value<Px>, pub blur: Value<Px>,   // x: physical, not mirrored
                         pub spread: Value<Px>,                // may be negative (below; ADD-A135)
                         pub color: Value<Color>, pub inset: bool,   // in right-to-left (S2.4)
                         pub falloff: ShadowFalloff,    // how its edge fades over `blur` (below; ADD-A134)
                         pub corner_radius: Option<Value<Px>> }  // None: the part's corners, changed by
                                                        // `spread`; Some: one circular radius on all four
                                                        // corners, which `spread` leaves (below; ADD-A136)
pub enum ShadowFalloff { Gaussian,             // CSS's: a Gaussian blur, its deviation half of `blur`
                         KirigamiSmoothstep }  // Kirigami's `ShadowedRectangle`: a smoothstep band, `blur` its
                                               // `shadow.size`
```

**Layer order** (ADD-A141; the GN-C1 verifier's question). `Layers` lists its layers bottom first, as `Paint`
does (S2.3), each painted over the ones before it, so the model has one order for every list of layers; the layers
without `inset` are painted beneath the part's fill and the inset layers over it, beneath its stroke, as CSS paints a
`box-shadow` (W3C CSS Backgrounds and Borders Level 3, *Drop Shadows*; the part's whole order is S2.11's *Drawing
order*). A CSS `box-shadow` list paints its first
shadow on top, so a fact states it reversed (libadwaita's `0 0 0 1px $border_color, 0 1px 3px 1px …, 0 2px 6px 2px
…` the widest layer first); material-web's elevation, its `::before` shadow beneath its `::after`, is already bottom
first. A part a platform draws from two nodes of one box (GTK's menu button, the outer `menubutton` node and its inner
button, `menubutton.card > button`) states the outer node's layers first and the inner node's after them, as the
inner node is painted over the outer. Rejected: CSS's order, first on top (one lane's sources, against `Paint`'s and
material-web's order, so a connector would read two orders); no stated order (the GNOME and Material facts already
disagree).

**Blur and falloff** (ADD-A134). `blur` is CSS's blur radius: under `Gaussian` the layer's shape (the part's
outline moved by `x` and `y`, grown by `spread`, or shrunk where `inset`) is blurred by a Gaussian whose standard
deviation is half of `blur`, as CSS's `box-shadow` defines it (W3C CSS Backgrounds and Borders Level 3, *Shadow
blurring*, followed directly), Breeze's shadow renderer computes it (`breeze@6.8.2
libbreezecommon/breezeboxshadowrenderer.cpp:34-38`, the deviation `radius * 0.5`, citing CSS, then approximated by
box blurs, `:27-32`); material-web's elevations and libadwaita's shadows are written as CSS `box-shadow`s. Under
`KirigamiSmoothstep` the layer is drawn as Kirigami's `ShadowedRectangle` draws its shadow: its alpha a smoothstep of
the signed distance to the shape, across a band centred on the shape's edge and with its corners rounded further, the
band and the rounding derived by the shader from `shadow.size`, the offset and the item's size, not a Gaussian
(`kirigami@6.31.0 src/primitives/shaders/shadowedrectangle.frag:34-45`; the uniforms,
`src/primitives/shadowedrectangle.cpp:355-375`), so `blur` is that `shadow.size`. Kirigami's shadow has no spread and is never inset, so S12 refuses a
`KirigamiSmoothstep` layer whose `spread` can be other than zero or whose `inset` is true. It is implemented once in
`native_theme::shapes` to that source, through the clean room, as it is LGPL (D10): `pub fn
kirigami_shadow_alpha(layer: &ResolvedShadowLayer, rect: Rect, corners: &OutlineCorners, at: Point) -> f32`, the
layer's coverage at a point for a part of that box and those corners (`ResolvedShadowLayer` the derive's resolved
layer, S6.1), which a connector drawing the shadow itself
calls, as it calls `outline` (S2.4); it is checked as a platform function is (S2.2's *Checked against their
references*): its vector table, `native-theme/tests/vectors/kirigami_shadow_alpha.tsv`, route
`compiled_source`, source `kirigami@6.31.0`, generation `kde-breeze`, rows of a `ShadowedRectangle`'s size,
corner radii, `shadow.size`, offset and a point, and the alpha the pinned shader, compiled unchanged into an offscreen
GL harness writing a float render target (`tools/kde-vectors`), draws there on a pinned renderer (Mesa's software
rasteriser at a version the table's header names), which the test `vectors_kirigami_shadow_alpha` and
`check_function_vectors.py` check within the tolerance the header states (ADD-A135; ledger queue #167): GLSL lets
built-in functions be inexact, and the item's antialiased edge comes from `fwidth` (`src/primitives/shaders/sdf.glsl:215-216`),
so the table cannot match bit for bit, the one generated table S2.2 lets state a tolerance. The coverage is the
shadow's band alone: inside the item's own shape the shader paints the item's fill over the shadow, replacing it
whatever the fill's alpha (`shadowedrectangle.frag:62-76`), so the table's points lie outside the shape's antialiased
edge; and the shader draws only inside the item's box grown on each side by `shadow.size` plus the
offset's length, each scaled by the box's aspect on that axis (`shadowedrectangle.cpp:18-35`), so the coverage is zero
beyond that area, where a large shadow is cut. Every layer states its `falloff` (`falloff = "gaussian"`): no default stands in
for a value (S1). A platform whose blur parameter means another thing states `blur` converted where a pinned source
gives the relation, else measured (S17). Matched layers (S2.7) whose falloffs differ interpolate as the old one
vanishing and the new one appearing. Rejected: a Gaussian approximation of Kirigami's band (a `blur` no source
gives, a visibly different edge); a generic `Smoothstep` band `blur` wide (Kirigami's band and corner rounding
follow the item's size and the offset too, which a band of its own width would lose); the falloff on `Shadow` rather than on each layer (a stack mixing two
falloffs could not be stated, and a layer's edge is the layer's).

The query resolves an elevation reference to that entry's layers, so a connector receives layers only, to draw and
to interpolate (a change of entry, WinUI's pressed control dropping from 2 to 1, W3-02, is a change of layers). A
reference to an empty entry resolves to `None`, as `Absent` does, so "no shadow" reaches the connector in one form; a
change to or from it interpolates as layers that appear or disappear do (S2.7). A part with `Ellipse` corners (S2.4)
casts each layer as the ellipse inscribed in that layer's own box (the part's box moved by `x` and `y`, grown by
`spread`, or shrunk by it where `inset`), as Breeze draws its round button's shadow with the button's radius on the
shadow's own rect, which Qt clamps per axis as it does the frame's (`breeze@6.8.2 kstyle/breezehelper.cpp:729-731`,
`:1654-1659`; `qtbase@6.12.0 src/gui/painting/qpaintengineex.cpp:745-746`; ADD-A124).

**A negative spread** (ADD-A135). `spread` may be negative (S1), as CSS's spread distance may: a negative one shrinks
an outer layer's shape on every side by its magnitude, its corners' radii less that distance, at least 0, as the model
takes radii less an inset, and grows an inset layer's inner shape by it, its radii growing by it; an outer layer
shrunk to no width or height casts nothing. Where a shape grows, its radii grow as S2.4's *Growing an outline*
says: a radius above zero by the whole distance, a zero radius not at all (a square corner stays square), as GTK
grows them (`gtk@4.24.1 gsk/gskroundedrect.c:217-236`), with CSS's factor for a radius below the spread rejected
there (ADD-A136; ledger queue #174 (1)). GTK moves the outline so (`gsk/gskroundedrect.c:259-296`: the sides moved,
the width and height floored at zero, each radius changed and floored at zero; an unblurred outset shadow's spread,
`gsk/gpu/gskgpunodeprocessor.c:1679`).

**A layer's own corner radius** (ADD-A136; ledger queue #174 (2)). A layer's shape takes the part's corners, changed
by its `spread` as above, unless the layer states `corner_radius`: then the shape's four corners are circular with
that radius, which the spread does not change, the spread moving its sides alone. Breeze's window and popup shadows
are such layers: each is rendered around a box with one radius of its own and placed by its padding so that the
box's edge lies `Shadow_Overlap` inside the surface's edge on every side, a spread of that overlap negated, while the
radius stays the surface's frame radius: a window's plus half a pixel, its overlap 3 px
(`breeze@6.8.2 kdecoration/breezedecoration.cpp:829`, the padding `:846-851`, `kdecoration/breeze.h:38`), a popup's
its frame radius, its overlap 2 px (`kstyle/breezeshadowhelper.cpp:205-208`, the padding `:225-228`,
`kstyle/breezemetrics.h:172`; the KDE facts' `spread_px = -2`, `docs/facts/kde/tokens.toml:1329-1452`). Under the
spread's rule those corners would be that radius less the overlap, 3.5 px smaller on a window and 2 px on a popup,
which moves each corner's arc inward by about 0.41 of that on its diagonal, 0.83 to 1.45 px, a move the layers' blurs
(6 px and up) soften but do not remove, so the facts state each such layer's `corner_radius`, an expression on the
frame radius the surface's own corners read. S12 refuses it on a `KirigamiSmoothstep` layer (Kirigami's shadow
follows the item's corners, `shadowedrectangle.frag:34-45`). In TOML a layer writes it `corner_radius_px`
(`corner_radius_px = "= add(…, 0.5px)"`); left out, the layer has none, as an `Option` in a list item is `None`
(S2.11). Matched layers (S2.7) interpolate it as one number on each corner, a layer without its own taking the radii
its spread gives the part's. Rejected: the full `Corners` form (four radii of any `Radius` variant and a curve, which
S12 would have to narrow to plain radii, while both sources set one radius, `breezedecoration.cpp:829`,
`breezeshadowhelper.cpp:208`, and one number interpolates simply); the difference recorded as a known inexactness
(the arc's move shows at the corners, and the model covers what is drawn); the KDE facts measuring the drawn shadow
and stating the layer that matches it best (no layer of the current fields matches it, so this is the inexactness
again, measured); an enum keeping or changing the part's radii (it cannot state the window's added half pixel); the
spread's rule changed to keep radii for every layer (GTK and CSS change them, and libadwaita's layers are drawn so);
the spread at least zero, with Breeze's overlap stated another way (no other field moves a layer's edges inward on
every side, and an inset layer is another shape).

### S2.6 Transform (R9)

```rust
pub struct Transform { pub scale_x: Value<f32>, pub scale_y: Value<f32>, pub rotate: Value<Deg>,
                       pub translate_x: Value<Px>, pub translate_y: Value<Px>,
                       pub origin: (f32, f32) }                // fractions of the part's box from its top-left
                                                               // corner, physical (below)
```

**How the components compose** (ADD-A146). As CSS's individual transform properties do (W3C CSS Transforms Level 2,
`translate`, `rotate` and `scale`, followed directly): about `origin`, the part is scaled, then rotated, then
translated, so the translation is in the layout's own axes, neither scaled nor rotated, and a part moved and turned
together is turned about its own origin and then moved. A positive `rotate` turns clockwise as drawn, y pointing
down, as S2.3's angles count; a source that counts the other way (a y-up coordinate system, AppKit's unflipped
views) is stated negated. A transition or a loop interpolates each component apart. Rejected: the components as
successive canvas calls in the struct's order (the translation would be scaled and turned with the part, where it
is a displacement in the layout, the reason it mirrors, below; the two readings differ as soon as two components
are set together).

A transform's translation is stated for a left-to-right layout and mirrored with it, as `Sides` and alignments are,
the one part of a part's drawing that mirrors (S1, S2.4, R16):
under right-to-left the query returns `translate_x` negated (S2.4), so a part moved toward its end moves toward the
end in either direction (an indeterminate bar's moving indicator, a thumb's offset). The reason is R16's: the toolkit
mirrors the layout, and a translation is a displacement in that layout, so stating it per direction would state one
motion twice. `origin`, `rotate`, `scale_x`, `scale_y` and `translate_y` are not mirrored: the origin is physical, as
the corners are (a fraction measured from the box's left edge in either direction), so a rotation or scale about an
origin off the centre is not mirrored either; a platform that does otherwise (a rotation reversed or an origin
mirrored under right-to-left, a translation kept) states it by a rule under the direction (S7). A scale of zero or
less on either axis draws nothing (no mirrored drawing: a shrinking dot's spring past zero, S2.7; ADD-A126).
